verses.1: Al-Mizan reads ‘ahead of God and His Messenger’ as the station of governance (ḥukm), shared by God and, by His permission, the Messenger, from which doctrine and practice are received. It therefore forbids placing one’s own rule, opinion, action, or even resolve before their ruling; every action and omission has a rule, including permissibility. The pairing with ‘all-hearing, all-knowing’ especially concerns opinions voiced or held inwardly, for God hears speech and knows what is public and concealed. Such obedience is entry into God’s wilāyah and servitude: the servant’s will conforms to His legislative will (tashrīʿ) as it does to His creative will (takwīn). The commentary rejects readings that confine the verse to physical precedence, speaking before the Prophet, or acting without his command, since these make God’s mention merely honorific rather than recognizing the joint governance indicated by the wording.
verses.2: Al-Mizan holds that raising one’s voice above the Prophet’s or addressing him as one addresses others violates the commanded reverence: it may display disdain amounting to kufr, or improper manners toward his rank. The apparent meaning makes both acts sins that can cause ḥabṭ, the failure of good works, rather than necessarily acts of disbelief in themselves. It rejects the view that only the reward of these particular acts is lost, since Qur’anic ḥabṭ connected with disbelief is likewise connected to deeds and an act’s invalidity entails the invalidity of its effects. It also rejects reducing the prohibition to a precaution against possibly grieving the Prophet; its wording directly forbids the acts themselves. ‘Without your being aware’ describes their condition before the warning: they could know the conduct was bad without knowing its grave consequence, but after revelation they know what it threatens.
verses.3: Al-Mizan explains that lowering one’s voice before God’s Messenger is the opposite of raising it and confirms the preceding prohibition by promising forgiveness and a great reward. Since God cannot test in order to discover an unknown state, His ‘trying’ hearts for Godwariness means training them or subjecting them to hardship until they acquire it. Calling him the Messenger identifies the basis of the ruling: reverence for one who conveys only from his Sender is reverence for God. The continuous form of ‘lower’ shows an established habit, revealing that Godwariness has become part of a person’s character; the promised forgiveness and reward answer that inward quality.
verses.4: Al-Mizan takes the call from behind the Prophet’s apartments as the uncivilized conduct of people who summoned him from outside his home without regard for proper manners or the duty to respect him. God’s description of most of them as failing to apply reason is therefore censure of that behavior as brutish.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says that waiting without shouting until the Prophet came out would have been better because it would have shown both good manners and respect for his position, bringing them nearer to God’s forgiveness and mercy. ‘All-forgiving, all-merciful’ may relate to this patience, or to the preceding lack of reason: their ignorant bad manners can be forgiven because they arose from deficient understanding.
verses.6: Al-Mizan defines a fāsiq as one who has departed obedience for sin, a nabaʾ as an important report, and tabayyan as verifying or making a matter clear. The command requires investigation of such a sinner’s report so that people are not harmed ignorantly and left regretful. It thereby affirms reliance on trustworthy reports, a rational practice indispensable to social life, while showing that an untrusted informant’s report lacks ḥujjiyyah. A multiply attested report, or one accompanied by decisive contextual indicators, is authoritative; hadith scholars treat a solitary report as authoritative only when its source is trustworthy, even if its particular content cannot independently be proved. Because the verse’s stated aim is removal of ignorance and attainment of knowledge before acting, the commentary regards it as God’s endorsement (imḍāʾ) of an established rational practice, not the founding of a new one.
verses.7: Al-Mizan links this verse to the command to verify a sinner’s report. The Messenger is among the faithful, supported by God and following guidance rather than their desires; they must refer matters to him, obey him, and not press him to follow their opinions, for his obedience to them in many matters would bring them toil and ruin. God’s making faith beloved and beautiful to their hearts, and faithlessness, transgression, and disobedience hateful, rescues them from that perversity as a divine gift. The commentary distinguishes fusūq as departure from obedience—here possibly deceit in the preceding report—from ʿiṣyān, disobedience more generally. Love of faith and aversion to these opposites constitute rushd, which they must retain by following the Messenger; the verse praises those who possess these traits while urging others among them to attain them. It also reads the wording as alluding to people who wanted reliance on the fāsiq al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah’s report concerning Banū Muṣṭalaq, though the revelation prevented the proposed attack.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains that God’s endearing faith, beautifying it in believers’ hearts, and making faithlessness, transgression, and disobedience hateful is sheer grace and blessing, not a return for anything they have done. Yet it is not arbitrary: God bestows such gifts wisely, in accordance with the purpose for which their recipients are worthy.
verses.9: Al-Mizan notes that the plural verb for the two groups’ fighting concerns their many individual members, while the dual in making peace concerns the two groups themselves; it reports the further explanation that fighters mingle as one mass, whereas peacemaking distinguishes the two sides. Baghī is unjust hostility, and fighting the aggressor continues until it returns (fayʾ) to God’s ordinance. Once it does, reconciliation must be just: not merely an end to arms, but implementation of God’s law concerning blood, honor, property, and every right the aggressor violated. Iqsāṭ is giving each person their due, and the command to do justice reinforces this qualified peace; God’s love for the just supplies further emphasis and rationale.
verses.10: Al-Mizan calls the faithful’s brotherhood a legislative declaration that establishes their relation and grounds both the combatants’ duty to reconcile and every other believer’s duty to make peace between them; Godwariness addresses both parties and mediators. It distinguishes natural kinship from conventional relationships whose effects are fixed by law: the latter may overlap with nature, but their legal force follows the relevant convention, not biological fact alone. Thus Islamic brotherhood can carry marriage and inheritance consequences; milk-brotherhood affects marriage but not inheritance; and religious brotherhood has social consequences without either of those legal effects. The commentary therefore rejects treating this verse’s brotherhood as a mere metaphor drawn from common parents or common faith. Its scope is determined by the legislative purpose it serves, as a conventional meaning may share all, some, or contextually varying effects of its literal analogue.
verses.11: Al-Mizan defines ridicule (sakhriyyah) as demeaning another by words, gestures, acts, or imitations that make others laugh. The verse separately names women because mockery commonly occurs within each sex, and its reason is that the mocked person may be better before God than the mocker. ‘Do not defame yourselves’ treats believers as one community, so defaming another is in effect defaming oneself. Nabz denotes offensive nicknames, such as ‘sinner’ or ‘fool’; ‘profane names after faith’ can mean disgraceful mention of a believer, marking one with an evil quality after belief, or making a name for oneself by insulting others. Each reading opposes associating believers with shame rather than good. Those who do not repent by regretting these sins and abandoning them are wrongdoers, which indicates that some believers had committed them.
verses.12: Al-Mizan understands the forbidden suspicion as ill thought (ẓann al-sūʾ), while thinking well is recommended. The prohibition concerns allowing an unwanted suspicion to affect conduct—by accusation, disclosure, belittling, or slander—not the involuntary thought itself, unless one actively entertains it. ‘Much suspicion’ may identify the sinning kind as a substantial category, or urge precaution against suspicion generally lest one fall into sin. Tajassus is negatively charged prying into private faults, unlike positively charged taḥassus. Ghibah is mention behind a person’s back of what he would dislike said, though public sins of an open sinner are excluded. Backbiting destroys a person’s social standing and, cumulatively, trust, safety, and the life of society; this explains the image of eating a dead brother’s flesh, whose death signifies his unawareness and whose brotherhood limits the rationale to Muslims. The image may also explain the ban on spying, which discovers faults directly rather than through another. Godwariness here may command repentance from these sins, with God accepting it in forgiveness, or avoidance of them, with His prior turning granting success and protection; divine tawbah can precede the servant’s repentance or follow it by accepting it.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains shuʿūb as nations and qabāʾil as tribes, while recording differing lexical accounts of their relative size and whether the former denotes non-Arabs and the latter Arabs. It reads the verse as denying superiority based on lineage: if ‘a male and a female’ means Adam and Eve, nations and tribes exist for mutual recognition, cooperation, and social life, not ancestral boasting. If it means men and women generally, the verse more universally overturns class distinctions of race, wealth, status, sex, and the like; the first reading better fits a specific condemnation of lineage-boasting, while the second is broader. Such differences enable society rather than confer honor or license one group to dominate another. True nobility before God is taqwā, the only path to lasting felicity near the Lord; worldly wealth, beauty, rank, lineage, and fame are illusory honors that lead to perdition. Unlike worldly competitions, all can seek this divine nobility without antagonism. God’s all-knowing awareness confirms that He, rather than human illusion, has chosen the true human goal and the way of Islam that leads to it.
verses.14: Al-Mizan limits the rebuke to some Bedouins who claimed faith, not all of them. God denies that īmān has entered their hearts while affirming their outward Islam, yet ‘not yet’ leaves open that faith may later enter. Īmān is inward conviction in divine unity, the Messenger’s truth, and his message; Islam is verbal and bodily submission through the testimonies and outward practice, whether or not inward conviction is present. This outward profession sanctifies life and governs marriage and inheritance. Sincere obedience requires inward and outward agreement without nifāq: obedience to God’s beliefs and practices and to the Messenger’s commands in the affairs under his authority. God will not diminish the recompense of such works, because He is all-forgiving and all-merciful.
verses.15: Al-Mizan takes the verse as a complete, exclusive definition of true believers: they have heartfelt conviction in God’s unity, the truth brought by His Messenger, and his messengership, and follow his commands. Their certainty persists without doubt; the use of thumma suggests an enduring, continually fresh firmness, unlike wording that would say only that they initially did not doubt. Their jihād with possessions and persons means exerting themselves in the way of God’s religion through every monetary obligation, such as zakāt and other payments, and bodily obligation, such as prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage. Those who combine these qualities are truthful in claiming faith; anyone lacking one is not truly within this definition.
verses.16: Al-Mizan reads this as a rebuke to the Bedouins who claimed, and then insisted, that they possessed faith. In response to their assertion after the preceding description of true believers, the verse asks how they can inform God of faith when His knowledge encompasses everything in the heavens and earth.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says that those who treat their embrace of Islam as a favor err twice. The real favor is īmān, which brings happiness in this world and the Hereafter, rather than Islam’s outward benefits of inviolable life, marriage, and inheritance; and the Prophet is only the messenger charged to convey God’s religion, so they have not benefited him. Nor can Islam be a favor to God, who is needless and whose servants alone gain from the religion. God has instead favored them by guiding them to faith, the true benefit, while their Islam benefits them only outwardly.
verses.18: Al-Mizan presents this closing verse as the ultimate rationale for the sūrah’s commands, prohibitions, descriptions of realities, and reports that some people possess faith while others do not. God knows the Unseen contained in the heavens and earth, and possibly what lies beyond them, and sees human deeds.
